Little white-shouldered bat Ametrida centurio is a small-bodied frugivore from the Neotropics, and its physiological attributes reflect the constraints of its diminutive size. Basal oxygen consumption, determined through respirometry trials on post-absorptive individuals resting in thermoneutral conditions at 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], averages 21.90 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 21.90 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This metabolic rate, measured as the maximum basal metabolic rate, is consistent with the elevated mass-specific energy demands typical of small chiropterans, whose high surface-area-to-volume ratios necessitate substantial heat production. Newborn pups emerge weighing approximately 2.8 grams [Wwb = approximately 2.8 grams], a value inferred from the closely related species Anoura caudifer given the difficulty of capturing pregnant females in the field. This minimal neonatal mass, representing only a fraction of adult size, suggests an altricial developmental pattern in which the mother bears the energetic burden of lactation for an extended period following parturition.

Reproductive output in Ametrida centurio is modest, constrained by the energetic ceilings imposed by small body size and a frugivorous diet that varies seasonally in availability. Females produce a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter] and complete just one litter each year [F_R_i = one litter each year], a reproductive tempo that aligns with the slow life-history strategies documented in many Neotropical bats at stable thermoneutral body temperatures near 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. The daily implications of this annual schedule are that each female contributes, on average, a single offspring annually, reflecting a strategy that prioritizes offspring quality over numerical quantity. This low reproductive frequency likely buffers the population against years of poor fruit abundance, as the energetic investment per pup can be maximized during favorable conditions.

Sexual size dimorphism is pronounced in this species, with adult females attaining a substantially larger asymptotic body mass than males. The ultimate wet weight for females reaches 12 grams [Wwi = 12 grams], representing a considerable investment in body reserves that supports gestation and lactation. In contrast, adult males plateau at a maximum recorded body mass of 8 grams [Wwi = 8 grams], a value that yields a female-to-male mass ratio of 1.5. This degree of dimorphism is among the highest recorded within the Stenodermatinae and likely reflects selection for increased female capacity to sustain the energetic costs of reproduction. Male body mass remains stable throughout the year, while females exhibit significant pre-partum weight gain as they accumulate the resources necessary for successful parturition.

Developmental timing in Ametrida centurio is strongly temperature-dependent, with key life-history milestones occurring under specific thermal regimes typical of the species' roosting environment. Gestation proceeds over an interval of 122 days [tg = 122 days] when mothers maintain a body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], a duration that is relatively prolonged for a bat of this size and may reflect the constraints of a low-energy fruit diet during pregnancy. Following birth, pups begin the process of weaning after approximately 30.5 days [tx = approximately 30.5 days] at the same maternal temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This relatively rapid transition to nutritional independence likely reduces the daily metabolic burden on the lactating female, allowing her to regain body condition before the next breeding season begins.

This maximum lifespan is noteworthy for a bat weighing no more than a dozen grams and suggests a slow pace of aging relative to similarly sized terrestrial mammals. The delay between weaning and reproductive maturation likely reflects the time required for juveniles to develop the flight skills and foraging efficiency necessary to sustain the energetic demands of pregnancy and lactation.
